question: How does EvidenceMem combine retrieval and text evidence?
quick: The classifier combines reliability-weighted visual retrieval with text-label similarity from a frozen vision-language representation.
standard:
The classifier combines reliability-weighted visual retrieval with text-label similarity from a frozen vision-language representation.

The memory stores real training examples near cluster centers, so retrieved evidence can be inspected. Classification computes visual and text components, then returns scores, confidence and an unknown flag. It does not retrain the encoder when adding memory entries.

The useful distinction is between learning a new representation and changing the evidence used for classification. Here the encoder stays frozen, while the memory provides examples against which a new image can be compared. Using actual examples near cluster centers makes the retrieved support inspectable: a user can see which training images influenced the decision.

The visual and text components can complement each other when one signal is weak, but their agreement is not a correctness guarantee. A visually similar example may share a background rather than the class-defining feature, and a text label may be ambiguous.

A medoid is an actual example; a centroid is an average. Unknown thresholds must be selected using validation data. The README explicitly limits performance claims, so do not describe memory retrieval as universally better than supervised baselines.

I would compare visual-only, text-only, and fused scores with the same frozen encoder. Unknown detection needs examples outside the known classes and a validation-selected threshold. Memory size changes both coverage and retrieval cost, so it belongs in the evaluation. The README's stated limitations should remain visible rather than being replaced with a blanket claim that memory-based classification outperforms supervised learning.
mistake: Treating nearest-neighbor similarity as calibrated confidence.

question: What did you personally implement in EvidenceMem?
quick: I need to connect my own contribution to specific files, commits and decisions before giving this answer.
standard:
I need to connect my own contribution to specific files, commits and decisions before giving this answer.

Use the source links to identify the execution path, then name the part you owned and what changed. Repository ownership alone does not establish sole authorship, the hardest bug, a team disagreement or the outcome of an experiment.

A confirmed contribution could be the memory-selection procedure, the score-fusion logic, or the presentation of retrieved evidence. I would choose the part I actually owned and explain the concrete problem it solved. For example, selecting representative real images has a different purpose from optimizing nearest-neighbor latency, even though both involve the memory.

The strongest supporting artifact would show the input, the chosen memory entries, the resulting scores, and the behavior that changed. That makes the contribution understandable without inventing a benchmark or attributing every component to one person.

Prepare a concrete before/after example, the relevant commit, a test or experiment and one limitation. Say “the project implements” for verified code and “I implemented” only for work you can personally confirm. Leave numerical results out until tied to a run artifact.

question: Walk through how EvidenceMem classifies an image using visual and text evidence.
quick: The memory stores real training examples near cluster centers, so retrieved evidence can be inspected. Classification computes visual and text components, then returns scores, confidence and an unknown flag. It does not retrain the encoder when adding memory entries.
standard:
The memory stores real training examples near cluster centers, so retrieved evidence can be inspected. Classification computes visual and text components, then returns scores, confidence and an unknown flag. It does not retrain the encoder when adding memory entries.

I would trace one image through the pipeline: create its frozen representation, compare it with stored visual evidence, compute the text-label component, and combine the scores using the implemented reliability logic. The returned class, confidence, and unknown flag should then be tied to those values.

Along the way I would check normalization and class ordering. A correct similarity calculation can still produce a wrong class if memory labels or text-label columns are misaligned. Inspecting the retrieved examples helps distinguish a representation problem from an indexing or labeling bug.

question: How would you test and improve EvidenceMem?
quick: I would establish a reproducible baseline and test the specific failure boundary exposed by this implementation.
standard:
I would establish a reproducible baseline and test the specific failure boundary exposed by this implementation.

A medoid is an actual example; a centroid is an average. Unknown thresholds must be selected using validation data. The README explicitly limits performance claims, so do not describe memory retrieval as universally better than supervised baselines.

I would separate three questions: whether the memory represents each class, whether similarity retrieves appropriate examples, and whether the final decision handles uncertainty. A classification score alone cannot identify which stage failed. Error review should include the image, its nearest evidence, component scores, and the final prediction.

The evaluation would compare against simple frozen-encoder baselines and vary memory size. Thresholds would be chosen on validation data, then fixed for the held-out test, including unknown-class examples.

Keep the current implementation separate from the proposed improvement. Save representative inputs, expected outputs and a versioned configuration. Test normal inputs, malformed inputs and the failure case described above. For model outputs, include a held-out evaluation and inspect errors rather than treating a confidence field as proof.
